evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Republic of China, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary says 孩 is not separately included in Shuowen, but quotes the 咳 entry’s “old form 咳 written with 子” statement. It distinguishes the child’s-laugh reading from the noun for an infant or young child, and cites Mengzi’s 孩提之童 and Li Mi’s Jin-era 生孩六月. Its entry documents uses, not a dated glyph sequence for 孩.
evidence.title: A00995 孩 — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Received Shuowen Jiezi and Duan Yucai’s commentary, transcribed at Shuowen.org
evidence.field: 咳 entry; graphic and lexical account
evidence.text: The received entry defines 咳 as a young child’s laugh, analyzes it as 口 plus phonetic 亥, and gives 孩 as an old form written with 子 instead of 口. Duan Yucai says Liji · Neize and Mengzi use this spelling. This supports a historical spelling relation between 孩 and 咳, but does not establish that the child noun developed from the laugh word.
evidence.title: 說文解字「咳」

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 子; early forms and semantic role
evidence.text: The database describes oracle-bone and bronze forms of 子 as depictions of infants, with forms emphasizing a large head and moving arms. It reports uses for children and other early uses, including borrowing for earthly-branch notation. This makes 子 semantically suitable in 孩, though it is evidence about the component, not an early inscription of the compound.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 子

evidence.text: The inspected record lists oracle-bone and bronze exemplars for 子 and describes it as an infant pictograph. It supports the component’s early graphic history, not an early compound 孩 form. The site states that its records are all rights reserved, so this record is cited only as evidence and is not proposed as an image asset.
evidence.title: 漢字「子」：字形演變

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database reports that the original referent of 亥 is unresolved. It discusses a buried-root proposal associated with Xu Shen and later scholars, and a pig-like or 豕-related proposal, while noting problems with both. It separately records later use as the twelfth earthly branch and confusion between 亥 and 豕 in copying. The uncertainty about 亥’s original referent does not undermine evidence for its later phonetic role in 孩.
evidence.title: 漢字甲骨部件分析 — 亥

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014) reconstruction tables
evidence.field: 孩 and 亥; pronunciation comparison and phonetic analysis
evidence.text: The entry analyzes 孩 as semantic 子 plus phonetic 亥. Mandarin is hái; the cited systems give Zhengzhang Old Chinese *ɡɯː for 孩 and *ɡɯːʔ for 亥, and Baxter–Sagart *[ɡ]ˤə and *[ɡ]ˤəʔ respectively. The close match within each named reconstruction system supports a phonetic relationship. These are reconstructions of the character readings, not a recovered spoken name for a depicted object in 亥.
evidence.title: 孩 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Wiktionary, citing Zhengzhang Shangfang (2003) and Baxter–Sagart (2014) reconstruction tables
evidence.text: Mandarin is hài. The entry gives Zhengzhang Old Chinese *ɡɯːʔ and Baxter–Sagart *[ɡ]ˤəʔ for 亥, compared with the corresponding reconstructed 孩 forms that lack the final glottal stop. It describes the graph’s original referent as uncertain. Phonological comparison supports the sound-component analysis without recovering the name of the depicted object.
evidence.title: 亥 — Wiktionary

evidence.source: Ministry of Education, Republic of China, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary’s research note quotes the Shuowen account: 咳 means a young child’s laugh and is written from 口 with 亥 as phonetic; 孩 is its old-form spelling with 子. This is a received lexicographic account, not independent proof of a pre-Han graphic sequence.
evidence.title: A00570 咳 — Ministry of Education Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants

evidence.source: Chinese Text Project, Mengzi · Jinxin I
evidence.text: The opened text contains 孩提之童 in the passage on children’s innate knowledge of affection for their parents. This provides a textual citation for the child-related expression, but the page does not date the character’s first use or establish a semantic derivation from the child’s-laugh sense.
evidence.title: 孟子 : 盡心上 : 15

evidence.source: Academia Sinica Center for Digital Cultures, Xiaoxuetang overview
evidence.text: The official overview says Xiaoxuetang covers oracle-bone, bronze, Warring States, small-seal, and regular forms. An attempted direct query for 子 could not be opened through the web tool, so no Xiaoxuetang glyph image is proposed.
evidence.title: 小學堂文字學資料庫簡介

evidence.text: The Commons page identifies the file as a vector representation of a bronze-script form of 子. The glyph is a modern drawing rather than a photograph of an ancient bronze object; the page states public-domain status for the drawing and script.

gaps: No inspected source provides a dated oracle-bone, bronze, or manuscript form of the compound 孩 itself; component forms must not be turned into a chronological sequence for the whole graph.

Shuowen records 孩 as an old spelling of the child’s-laugh word 咳, while later sources attest 孩 as child/infant. The available evidence does not establish whether the noun developed semantically from laughter, was a parallel lexical use, or involved both.

The exact earliest dated attestation of the 孩 child noun was not established. The inspected sources cite Mengzi, Liji, and a Jin-era memorial but do not provide a securely dated original manuscript witness for each quotation.

No inspected primary paleographic source resolves the original pictured referent or spoken name of 亥. Reconstructions compare the readings of 孩 and 亥; they do not recover a name for a plant, pig, or other depicted object.
Smith’s proposed root/germ word family and derivation of 孩 as “sprout” remain proposals; the cited summary notes that this sense is unattested and the derivation unexplained.

A direct Xiaoxuetang query could not be opened through the web tool; therefore no exact query glyph or candidate image is offered. Sinica’s inspected chardb page is all rights reserved and is not used as an image asset.
Modern multi-language readings were outside the focus of this verification; the directly checked pronunciation comparison covers Mandarin and two Old Chinese reconstruction systems.

items.period: Shang dynasty, oracle-bone script style; source description gives style, not an independently dated artifact image
items.caption: A modern vector redraw of 子 in Shang oracle-bone script style. Early 子 forms depict an infant; this is a component comparison, not an attested early form of 孩.
items.alt: Black vector outline of a single oracle-bone-style character 子 on a plain background.
items.selection_reason: Shows the early form tradition and infant-related component used semantically in the later graph 孩; it is explicitly a modern redraw.
items.rights: CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication, as stated on the Commons file page.

items.period: Bronze-script tradition; Commons page does not assign a specific dated inscription
items.caption: A modern vector drawing of a bronze-script 子 form, included to show the historical component tradition. It is not an ancient artifact photograph, and it does not document a bronze inscription of 孩.
items.alt: Black vector outline of a single bronze-script-style character 子 on a plain background.
items.selection_reason: A second reusable example shows the same meaning component in bronze-script style without implying that the whole compound 孩 is attested at that date.
items.rights: Public domain dedication for the vector representation and ancient script, stated on the Commons file page.

limitations.text: These selected images show 子 forms only. No usable early glyph image for 孩 itself was identified, so the images should illustrate component background rather than a sequence in the compound’s graphic history.
Both are modern redrawings of script forms, not photographs of inscribed oracle bones or bronzes. Their particular exemplars should not be treated as dated artifacts.
